course.title: Agile & Scrum
course.description: A practical tour of how modern teams plan and deliver work in short, inspectable cycles, from the Agile Manifesto to the roles, events, and artifacts of Scrum. You will learn why iterative delivery often beats a single big plan, how to size and order a backlog, and how to read velocity and burndown without fooling yourself. Structure adapted from the article on agile software development at Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: The Agile Manifesto is built on how many core values?
questions.explanation: The Manifesto states four values; it also lists twelve supporting principles - see 'Why agile, and the Manifesto'.

questions.prompt: Scrum is best described as...
options: a fixed project plan written up front
a lightweight framework for delivering work in short iterations
questions.explanation: Scrum is a lightweight framework built on short cycles with inspection and adaptation.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for maximizing product value and ordering the product backlog?
questions.explanation: The Product Owner owns the backlog and its ordering - see 'Scrum roles'.

questions.prompt: A sprint in Scrum is a fixed timebox of...
questions.explanation: Sprints are short, consistent cycles of one month or less.

questions.prompt: The daily scrum mainly exists for...
options: the Developers to plan the next day of work toward the sprint goal
questions.explanation: It is a short planning event owned by the Developers, not a status meeting.

questions.prompt: Story points estimate...
options: the exact number of hours a task will take
the relative size and effort of a backlog item
the dollar cost of the work
how many people are on the team
questions.explanation: Points are a relative, not absolute, measure of size and effort.

questions.prompt: The definition of done is...
options: a shared checklist of quality criteria every increment must meet
the same thing as the sprint goal
questions.explanation: It is a shared, agreed standard of quality for a releasable increment.

questions.prompt: Compared with the waterfall approach, agile methods favor...
options: one large release at the very end
responding to change over rigidly following a fixed plan
questions.explanation: Agile prizes adapting to change and delivering value early and often.

lessons.title: Why agile exists, and the Manifesto
lessons.grammar_note: Agile is an adjective and a mindset, not a noun you can finish - say 'working in an agile way,' not 'we completed agile.'

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why agile ways of working emerged, contrast them with the traditional waterfall approach, and name the four values and the shape of the twelve principles in the Agile Manifesto. By the end you should be able to argue, in plain language, when short iterations beat a single big plan - and when a heavier process still makes sense. Warm-up: picture a team that spends six months building a product nobody sees until launch day, then learns at launch that the customer needed something quite different. What did that long silence cost them in money and in trust? How might delivering a small, working slice every few weeks have surfaced the mismatch while it was still cheap to fix? Hold that question in mind; the rest of the lesson is really one long answer to it. Agile is less a toolkit than a bet that feedback beats forecasting when the future is uncertain.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Waterfall runs a project as a strict sequence: gather all requirements, design everything, build everything, then test and release once at the end. That works when requirements are stable and well understood, but software requirements rarely are. By the time a long build finishes, the market, the users, or the understanding of the problem have usually moved, and a wrong guess made in month one is not discovered until month twelve, when it is expensive to undo. Agile methods respond by shrinking the loop. Teams deliver small, working increments on a short, regular cadence, show them to real users, and let what they learn reshape the plan. In 2001 a group of practitioners wrote the Agile Manifesto, which names four values: individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; and responding to change over following a plan. The phrasing matters - the things on the right still have value, but the things on the left have more. Twelve principles expand on this, stressing early and continuous delivery, welcoming change, short timescales, daily collaboration, sustainable pace, technical excellence, simplicity, and regular reflection.

sections.heading: Key practices & examples
sections.text: Read the four values as trade-offs under pressure, not as permission to drop the right-hand items. 'Working software over comprehensive documentation' does not mean no documentation; it means a running feature that users can try teaches you more than a thick spec that nobody has validated. Example: instead of a 40-page requirements document, a team ships a rough checkout flow in two weeks and watches ten users stumble at the same step - a lesson no document would have given. 'Responding to change over following a plan' shows up as a backlog that is reordered every few weeks as priorities shift, rather than a locked scope. Among the twelve principles, the most quoted is the first: satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software. Another, often forgotten, warns that agile teams should keep a sustainable pace indefinitely, not sprint themselves into burnout. Note too that 'agile' is an umbrella: Scrum, Kanban, and Extreme Programming are all agile approaches that share these values but differ in mechanics. This course focuses on Scrum, the most widely used, while borrowing ideas from Kanban later.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four values of the Agile Manifesto in the 'X over Y' form. 2) True or false: 'working software over comprehensive documentation' means documentation is banned. 3) Give one situation where waterfall is a reasonable choice. 4) Which Manifesto principle concerns the team's long-term energy? 5) Is Scrum the same thing as agile? Answers: 1) individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan. 2) False - it means prefer a working product as the measure of progress; some documentation is still useful. 3) When requirements are truly fixed and well understood, such as a regulated build with a frozen, contracted specification. 4) The principle of maintaining a sustainable, constant pace indefinitely. 5) No - Scrum is one agile framework among several, including Kanban and Extreme Programming.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading the Manifesto as 'no plans, no docs, no process.' The values rank priorities; they do not delete the lower-ranked item. Teams that skip all documentation and planning are not agile, just disorganized. Mistake: treating agile as a fixed recipe to install rather than a set of values you apply with judgment. Mistake: confusing 'responding to change' with having no direction - a clear goal still steers each iteration. Exit: (a) How many values and how many principles does the Agile Manifesto contain? (b) In one sentence, what is the core bet agile makes about uncertain projects? Answers: four values and twelve principles; that frequent feedback on small, working increments beats trying to forecast and plan the whole project in advance.

lessons.title: The Scrum framework and its roles
lessons.grammar_note: Scrum is a proper noun and is capitalized; a 'sprint' and the 'daily scrum' are common nouns in lowercase unless they start a sentence.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe Scrum as a framework built on short cycles and empirical control, and explain the three accountabilities on a Scrum Team: the Product Owner, the Scrum Master, and the Developers. You will be able to say who decides what gets built, who protects the way of working, and who does the building - and why keeping those separate matters. Warm-up: on teams you have seen, who decided what to build next, and was that the same person who did the work? When one person both sets priorities and writes the code under deadline pressure, which side tends to suffer? Scrum deliberately splits these jobs so that value decisions and delivery decisions each have a clear owner, and so that the health of the process itself is somebody's explicit responsibility rather than nobody's.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Scrum is a lightweight framework for developing complex products. It rests on empiricism: because you cannot fully predict a complex project, you proceed in short cycles, inspect the result, and adapt. Three pillars support this - transparency, inspection, and adaptation. The work happens in sprints, fixed timeboxes of a month or less, each producing a usable increment. A Scrum Team is small, typically ten people or fewer, and cross-functional, meaning it holds all the skills needed to deliver. There is no sub-team hierarchy and no separate project manager. Instead there are three accountabilities. The Product Owner is accountable for the value of the product and owns the product backlog, deciding what is built and in what order. The Scrum Master is accountable for the team's effectiveness, coaches Scrum, facilitates events, and removes impediments that block progress. The Developers are the people who build the increment - writing, testing, and integrating the work - and they own how they turn backlog items into done increments each sprint. One Product Owner, one Scrum Master, and the Developers together form the whole team.

sections.heading: Key practices & examples
sections.text: Keep the roles distinct in practice. The Product Owner talks to stakeholders and users, shapes the backlog, and is a single person, not a committee, so priorities stay coherent - example: when sales and support both demand a feature next, the Product Owner makes the call and orders the backlog accordingly. The Scrum Master serves the team, the Product Owner, and the wider organization; a typical day might include facilitating the retrospective, helping the Product Owner split a vague request into clear items, and chasing down a licensing delay that is blocking the Developers. The Scrum Master leads by influence, not authority - they do not assign tasks. The Developers self-manage: they decide together how much to pull into a sprint and how to build it, rather than taking orders. A healthy sign is that the Developers, not a manager, forecast the sprint. A warning sign is a Scrum Master who behaves like a traditional boss, or a Product Owner who dictates technical design. Cross-functionality means the team should not have to hand work to an outside group to get it done.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which accountability owns the product backlog and its ordering? 2) Who removes impediments and coaches the team on Scrum? 3) Can one person hold both the Product Owner and Scrum Master roles well on the same team? 4) Who decides how much work to take into a sprint? 5) What does 'cross-functional' mean for a Scrum Team? Answers: 1) the Product Owner. 2) the Scrum Master. 3) It is discouraged - the roles can pull in opposite directions (value versus process health), so splitting them keeps each honest. 4) the Developers, by forecasting what they can complete. 5) the team holds all the skills needed to create a done increment without depending on an outside group.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: turning the Scrum Master into a status-chasing manager who assigns tasks - that undercuts the Developers' self-management. Mistake: running the Product Owner role as a committee, which produces a muddled, contradictory backlog. Mistake: expecting the Scrum Master to write the code or the Product Owner to design the architecture; each stays in their lane. Mistake: adding a separate project manager on top, which recreates the hierarchy Scrum removes. Exit: (a) Name the three accountabilities on a Scrum Team. (b) Which one is responsible for maximizing the value of the product? Answers: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers; the Product Owner is responsible for maximizing product value.

lessons.title: Scrum events: the sprint and its rhythm
lessons.grammar_note: Timeboxes are maximums, not targets - a daily scrum is 'at most 15 minutes,' so finishing in 8 is fine; running to 30 is not.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the five Scrum events and say what each is for, who owns it, and how long it should take. You will be able to lay out the rhythm of a sprint from planning through review and retrospective, and explain why each event exists to create an opportunity for inspection and adaptation rather than just to fill a calendar. Warm-up: think of a recurring meeting you have sat through that had no clear purpose or output. What made it feel like a waste, and what single question would have told the room whether it was worth holding? Each Scrum event answers a specific question - what will we do, are we on track, what did we build, and how can we work better - and if an event is not answering its question, that is the signal to fix it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The sprint is the container for all other events: a fixed timebox of a month or less, with a consistent length so the team settles into a steady cadence, and a new one starts the moment the last ends. Inside each sprint are four events. Sprint planning opens the sprint: the team agrees a sprint goal, the Product Owner presents the most valuable backlog items, and the Developers forecast what they can complete and draft a plan, producing the sprint backlog. The daily scrum is a short event, at most fifteen minutes, where the Developers inspect progress toward the sprint goal and plan the next day of work. The sprint review comes near the end: the team and stakeholders inspect the increment and discuss what to do next, adapting the product backlog. The sprint retrospective closes the sprint: the team inspects how it worked - process, tools, relationships - and commits to improvements. Timeboxes scale with sprint length; for a two-week sprint, planning is a few hours and the review and retrospective are shorter still.

sections.heading: Key practices & examples
sections.text: Treat each event by its output, not its ritual. Sprint planning should end with a clear sprint goal and a sprint backlog the Developers believe in - example: 'let users reset their password without contacting support' is a goal, not just a list of tickets. The daily scrum is for the Developers to re-plan, so a good one surfaces a blocker and someone volunteers to clear it; a bad one is each person reciting yesterday's tasks to the Scrum Master. Keep it to fifteen minutes and take deep discussions offline. The sprint review is a working session with stakeholders around a real, running increment, not a slide show - feedback here reshapes the backlog. The retrospective is where real improvement lives: pick one or two concrete changes the team will try next sprint, not a long wish list. A common healthy pattern is to end the retrospective with a single experiment and check next time whether it helped. Protect the sprint by not changing the sprint goal mid-sprint.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which event produces the sprint backlog? 2) What is the maximum length of the daily scrum? 3) Which event inspects the increment with stakeholders? 4) Which event focuses on improving how the team works? 5) When does the next sprint start after one ends? Answers: 1) sprint planning. 2) fifteen minutes. 3) the sprint review. 4) the sprint retrospective. 5) immediately - a new sprint begins right after the previous one concludes, with no gap.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: turning the daily scrum into a status report to a manager instead of the Developers' own planning session. Mistake: skipping the retrospective when things get busy - that removes the one event dedicated to getting better, exactly when it is most needed. Mistake: letting the sprint review become a polished demo with no real feedback or backlog changes. Mistake: extending the sprint to 'fit more in,' which breaks the steady cadence and hides problems. Exit: (a) List the five Scrum events. (b) Which event creates the sprint goal and the sprint backlog? Answers: the sprint, sprint planning, the daily scrum, the sprint review, and the sprint retrospective; sprint planning creates the sprint goal and the sprint backlog.

questions.prompt: Which phrase correctly completes an Agile Manifesto value?
options: following a plan over responding to change
questions.explanation: The value places working software above comprehensive documentation.

questions.prompt: On a Scrum Team, who facilitates the events and removes impediments?
questions.explanation: The Scrum Master coaches the team and clears blockers.

questions.prompt: Sprint planning primarily produces...
options: a sprint goal and a sprint backlog
questions.explanation: Planning sets the sprint goal and the Developers' forecast, the sprint backlog.

questions.prompt: The daily scrum is timeboxed to at most...
questions.explanation: It is a maximum of fifteen minutes for the Developers to re-plan.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for ordering the product backlog?
questions.explanation: The Product Owner owns and orders the backlog by value.

questions.prompt: The main purpose of the sprint review is to...
options: improve how the team works together
inspect the increment with stakeholders and adapt the backlog
plan the next day of work
questions.explanation: The review inspects the product increment and adapts what comes next; improving teamwork is the retrospective.

lessons.title: Scrum artifacts and the definition of done
lessons.grammar_note: 'Done' in Scrum is a defined state, not a feeling - an item is done only when it meets the definition of done, which is why the term is often written in quotes.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the three Scrum artifacts - the product backlog, the sprint backlog, and the increment - and explain the commitment attached to each, including the definition of done. You will be able to say where each artifact lives, who owns it, and how the definition of done keeps 'finished' from meaning different things to different people. Warm-up: imagine two developers each say their feature is 'done,' but one means 'it runs on my laptop' and the other means 'it is tested, reviewed, and deployed.' What goes wrong when the word carries two meanings? How would a shared, written standard for 'done' prevent that argument from happening every sprint? Artifacts exist to make work visible and to anchor shared agreements, so that transparency is built into the objects the team handles every day, not left to memory or hope.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Scrum defines three artifacts, each with a commitment that gives it focus. The product backlog is the single, ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product; it is owned by the Product Owner and is never truly finished, because it evolves as the product and its environment change. Its commitment is the product goal - the longer-term objective the backlog serves. The sprint backlog is the set of items the Developers selected for the current sprint plus a plan for delivering them and the sprint goal; it is owned by the Developers and updated throughout the sprint as they learn. Its commitment is the sprint goal. The increment is a concrete, usable step toward the product goal - the sum of all completed backlog items this sprint, added to everything done before, and it must be in working order. Its commitment is the definition of done: a shared, explicit set of quality criteria that an increment must meet to be considered releasable. Work that does not meet the definition of done is not part of the increment and goes back on the product backlog.

sections.heading: Key practices & examples
sections.text: Keep the product backlog ordered and visible, with the most valuable and well-understood items near the top and vaguer ideas lower down. Example: the top three items are small and clear enough to pull into the next sprint, while an item like 'improve onboarding' sits lower until it is refined. The sprint backlog belongs to the Developers; they add, drop, or re-plan tasks during the sprint as long as the sprint goal stays intact. The definition of done is the team's quality contract - a concrete checklist such as code reviewed, automated tests passing, documentation updated, and deployed to staging. Write it down and apply it to every item; an item is 'done' only when it ticks every box. Example: a feature that works but has no tests is not done, so it does not count toward the increment or the team's velocity. If the organization has a shared standard, the team's definition must meet or exceed it. A strong definition of done prevents a pile of 'almost finished' work from hiding real progress.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which artifact is the single ordered list of everything the product might need? 2) Who owns the sprint backlog? 3) What commitment is attached to the increment? 4) If an item passes review but has no tests, and the definition of done requires tests, is it done? 5) What happens to work that fails the definition of done at the sprint's end? Answers: 1) the product backlog. 2) the Developers. 3) the definition of done. 4) no - it must meet every criterion in the definition of done. 5) it is not part of the increment and returns to the product backlog for a future sprint.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: keeping multiple competing backlogs or an unordered wish list, so no one knows what is truly next. Mistake: letting managers stuff the sprint backlog, which strips the Developers of ownership. Mistake: treating 'done' as a personal judgment, so 'done' secretly means 'mostly done' and quality rots. Mistake: carrying undone work silently into the next sprint instead of returning it to the backlog honestly. Exit: (a) Name the three Scrum artifacts and the commitment tied to each. (b) In one sentence, why does a shared definition of done matter? Answers: product backlog (product goal), sprint backlog (sprint goal), increment (definition of done); it gives everyone one clear, shared standard for what 'finished' means, so progress is real and comparable.

lessons.title: User stories, story points, and backlog refinement
lessons.grammar_note: A user story is written from the user's view, not the system's - start with 'As a [user]' rather than 'The system shall,' which is waterfall-era phrasing.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write a user story in the common template, estimate backlog items with relative story points, and explain what backlog refinement and prioritization do between sprints. You will be able to turn a vague request into a small, testable story, size it against others instead of guessing hours, and order the backlog so the most valuable, ready work sits on top. Warm-up: a stakeholder says 'make the app faster.' Why is that hard to build or test as written? What would you need to ask to turn it into something a team could finish in a sprint and verify is done? Good backlog work is mostly this translation - from wishes into clear, right-sized, ordered items - and it is where a lot of a team's effectiveness is quietly won or lost.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A user story is a short description of a feature told from the user's point of view, often in the form: as a [type of user], I want [some goal] so that [some benefit]. The 'so that' clause keeps the team focused on value, not just mechanics. Stories should be small enough to finish within a sprint and come with acceptance criteria that make 'done' testable. Rather than estimating in hours, many teams size stories in story points - a relative measure of effort, complexity, and uncertainty. A point value only has meaning compared with other items: a five-point story is roughly five times the size of a one-point story. Teams often estimate together using planning poker, where everyone reveals a number at once and discusses the gaps, which surfaces hidden assumptions. Backlog refinement is the ongoing activity of breaking down large items, adding detail and acceptance criteria, and re-estimating, so that items near the top are small and ready. Prioritization orders the backlog by value, cost, risk, and dependencies so the team always pulls the most worthwhile ready work next.

sections.heading: Key practices & examples
sections.text: Write stories that are independent, small, and testable. Example: 'As a returning shopper, I want to save items for later so that I can buy them on my next visit,' with acceptance criteria listing where the saved list appears and how long items persist. Split epics - stories too big for one sprint - into thin vertical slices that each deliver something usable. For sizing, keep a reference story the team agrees is, say, three points, and estimate others against it; consistency matters more than precision. Planning poker helps: if estimates range from two to thirteen, the gap signals a misunderstanding worth discussing before the work starts. For prioritization, a simple approach weighs value against effort and pulls high-value, low-effort items forward, while watching dependencies so a blocked item does not sit at the top. Example: a one-point, high-value fix that unblocks three other stories belongs near the top. Refine a little each sprint rather than in one marathon session, keeping roughly a sprint or two of ready work at the top of the backlog.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Fill in the user story template: as a [ ], I want [ ] so that [ ]. 2) Do story points measure hours? 3) What is an epic? 4) Why do teams reveal planning-poker estimates simultaneously? 5) What is the goal of backlog refinement? Answers: 1) as a [type of user], I want [a goal] so that [a benefit]. 2) no - they measure relative size, effort, complexity, and uncertainty. 3) a story too large to finish in a single sprint, which must be split into smaller stories. 4) so early numbers do not anchor everyone else, keeping estimates independent and surfacing disagreement. 5) to keep top backlog items small, detailed, estimated, and ready to pull into a sprint.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing 'requirements' from the system's view ('the system shall...') instead of user-centered stories with a clear benefit. Mistake: converting story points straight into hours, which throws away the whole point of relative sizing. Mistake: estimating alone, so one person's blind spot becomes the team's. Mistake: hoarding a giant, unrefined backlog where the top items are still too big to start. Exit: (a) What are the three parts of the common user story template? (b) Name one factor, besides raw value, that should affect how you order the backlog. Answers: the user type, the goal, and the benefit ('so that'); dependencies (or cost, risk, or effort) - for example, pulling forward an item that unblocks others.

lessons.title: Metrics, Kanban, and scaling without the pitfalls
lessons.grammar_note: Velocity is a planning aid, not a score - compare a team only with itself over time, never one team's velocity against another's.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read velocity and a burndown chart without misusing them, describe how Kanban manages flow by limiting work in progress, and name the common traps teams hit when they try to scale Scrum across many teams. You will be able to use metrics to forecast and spot trouble rather than to rank people, and to recognize when 'doing Scrum' has quietly become theater. Warm-up: suppose a manager starts rewarding the team with the highest velocity. What do you predict happens to the point estimates over the next few sprints, and why does that make velocity useless as a cross-team score? Metrics shape behavior, so the value of any agile metric depends entirely on using it for learning and forecasting inside one team, not for comparison or pressure across teams.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Velocity is the amount of work, measured in story points, a team completes in a sprint, averaged over several sprints. Its honest use is forecasting: if a team averages thirty points and the next chunk of backlog totals ninety, that is roughly three sprints of work. Because points are relative and each team sets its own scale, velocity cannot compare teams. A burndown chart plots remaining work against time within a sprint; a line falling steadily toward zero suggests the team is on track, while a flat or rising line warns of a blocker or scope creep. Kanban is a related agile approach focused on flow: work items move across a board of columns, and each column has a work-in-progress limit that caps how many items can be in it at once. Limiting work in progress exposes bottlenecks and shortens the time an item takes to cross the board. Scrum and Kanban are often combined. Scaling Scrum to many teams on one product adds coordination needs, and frameworks exist for it, but scaling multiplies both the benefits and the dysfunctions of how a single team already works.

sections.heading: Key practices & examples
sections.text: Use velocity only to forecast and only within one team - example: after five sprints a team's velocity settles near twenty-five, so it plans the next sprint around that, not around a hopeful forty. Watch the trend, not a single sprint, since one noisy number means little. Read a burndown for shape: a long flat stretch mid-sprint usually means something is stuck, so investigate rather than wait. In Kanban, a work-in-progress limit of, say, three in the 'testing' column forces the team to finish testing before starting more, which reveals that testing, not coding, is the real bottleneck. For scaling, the reliable advice is to get one team genuinely healthy first; copying ceremonies across twenty teams without the underlying mindset just scales the dysfunction. Beware common pitfalls: 'zombie Scrum,' where events happen but nothing is inspected or changed; treating velocity as a performance target, which inflates estimates; skipping retrospectives; and a Product Owner who is unavailable, leaving the backlog unordered. The cure is almost always to return to the values - transparency, inspection, and adaptation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A team averages twenty points per sprint and faces one hundred points of backlog - roughly how many sprints is that? 2) Can you compare two teams by their velocity? 3) What does a flat burndown line in the middle of a sprint suggest? 4) What does a work-in-progress limit do in Kanban? 5) Name one common pitfall when scaling or running Scrum. Answers: 1) about five sprints. 2) no - each team sets its own point scale, so velocities are not comparable. 3) that work has stalled, often a blocker or hidden scope, and it needs investigating. 4) it caps how many items can sit in a column at once, exposing bottlenecks and improving flow. 5) 'zombie Scrum' / events with no real inspection, using velocity as a target, skipping retrospectives, or an absent Product Owner (any one).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using velocity to compare or rank teams, which rewards inflating estimates rather than delivering value. Mistake: reading a single sprint's velocity as a trend instead of averaging several. Mistake: adding Kanban columns without work-in-progress limits, so the board shows status but never improves flow. Mistake: scaling the mechanics of Scrum across many teams before one team works well, which just multiplies the problems. Exit: (a) State the one legitimate use of velocity. (b) What is the purpose of a work-in-progress limit? Answers: forecasting how much upcoming work a single team can complete over time; to cap concurrent work in a stage so bottlenecks become visible and items flow to done faster.

items.translation: a fixed timebox of one month or less in which a team produces a usable increment
items.example: The team runs two-week sprints, so a new one starts every other Monday.

items.translation: the single ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product, owned by the Product Owner
items.example: She moved the password-reset story to the top of the product backlog.

items.translation: the items the Developers selected for the current sprint plus their plan and the sprint goal
items.example: By day two the sprint backlog had shifted as the team learned more.

items.translation: a usable, working step toward the product goal that meets the definition of done
items.example: This sprint's increment let users log in with a one-time code.

items.translation: a shared checklist of quality criteria an item must meet to count as finished
items.example: No tests means it fails the definition of done, so it is not done.

items.translation: a short, user-centered description of a feature in the form 'as a user, I want a goal so that a benefit'
items.example: The user story explained why saving items for later would help shoppers.

items.translation: a relative measure of an item's size, effort, complexity, and uncertainty
items.example: They sized the search feature at eight story points against a known three-point story.

items.translation: the story points a single team completes per sprint, averaged over time and used only to forecast
items.example: With a velocity near twenty-five, they planned the next sprint around that figure.

questions.prompt: The product backlog differs from the sprint backlog in that the product backlog...
options: is owned by the Developers for one sprint
is the full ordered list of everything the product might need
questions.explanation: The product backlog is the single evolving ordered list; the sprint backlog is the current sprint's selected subset plus a plan.

questions.prompt: An item meets the definition of done only when...
options: it runs on one developer's machine
it satisfies every agreed quality criterion
questions.explanation: The definition of done is a shared checklist, and every criterion must be met.

questions.prompt: Story points are best understood as...
options: a relative measure of size and complexity
questions.explanation: Points size items relative to each other, not in absolute hours.

questions.prompt: Velocity can legitimately be used to...
options: forecast how much work a single team can finish over time
questions.explanation: Velocity is a single-team forecasting aid, not a cross-team or individual score.

questions.prompt: A burndown chart that stays flat through the middle of a sprint most likely signals...
options: work has stalled or there is a hidden blocker
questions.explanation: A flat line means remaining work is not dropping, suggesting a blocker or scope creep.

questions.prompt: In Kanban, a work-in-progress limit is used to...
options: cap concurrent items in a column so bottlenecks become visible
questions.explanation: Limiting work in progress exposes bottlenecks and improves flow to done.
